extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, editorial office staff, publishers, and COPE member organisations
extracted.subtask_description: Flowcharts and procedural guidance for journal editors and editorial offices on detecting, investigating, preventing, and responding to publication ethics problems (image manipulation, plagiarism, peer‑review manipulation, redundancy, authorship issues, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Image manipulation: evidence thresholds and actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on handling suspected or admitted image manipulation, distinguishing clear manipulation, unclear/suspected manipulation, and clear admission by authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If author clearly admits manipulation: apologise to author and publish correction if necessary (e.g., honest error that does not invalidate conclusions). If clear manipulation affecting integrity: publish a retraction (or consider correction if manipulation is very minor and majority of results/conclusions remain valid), contact all authors, tell them planned action, inform readers of outcome. If unclear/suspected: consider whether evidence (e.g., duplicated parts visible on zoom) is sufficient to publish a correction or retraction; consider using software to analyse images. If no satisfactory author response, contact the author’s institution requesting the concern be passed to the author’s superior/person responsible for research governance; consider contacting authorities (eg, ORI, GMC) and publishing an Expression of Concern. Consider contacting authors’ institutions every 3–6 months if ongoing investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical oversight: handling lack of approvals or consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure when reviewer or editor raises ethical concerns such as lack of ethical approval, patient consent/protection concerns, or animal experimentation issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thank the reviewer/editor and investigate. Request authors supply relevant details (eg, evidence of ethical committee/IRB approval or copies of informed consent). If response is satisfactory: proceed with review. If no or unsatisfactory response: inform the reviewer of outcome, consider suspending review until resolved, forward concerns to the author’s employer/person responsible for research governance at the institution. For COPE members, consider submitting the case to the COPE Forum if novel ethical issues arise. If no resolution, contact other authorities (eg, medical registration body, ORI) and inform the reviewer of outcome/action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism: check degree and respond proportionately
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess degree of copying and differentiate between clear plagiarism, redundancy (self‑plagiarism), and minor copying of short phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get full documentary evidence. Check degree of copying. For clear plagiarism (unattributed large portions of text/data presented as by the plagiarist): contact corresponding author in writing (ideally enclose signed authorship statement), attempt to contact all authors, consider rejection and informing author’s superior and/or person responsible for research governance and potential victims. Consider contacting other journals or publishers, and consider publishing a retraction. For redundancy/self‑plagiarism: see redundancy flowchart—contact author in neutral terms, request missing references or removal of overlapping material, consider correction with reference to original if legitimate republication. For minor copying of short phrases (eg, language issues for non‑native speakers): ask author to rephrase or include direct quotations with references; discuss with reviewer and proceed with review. Inform reviewer/reader of outcome and action taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual property / no response escalation
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps to take if authors do not respond or provide inconclusive replies when raised about intellectual property/plagiarism concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempt to contact all other authors (check Medline/Google for current affiliations/emails). If still no response, contact the author’s institution requesting the concern is passed to the author’s superior/person responsible for research governance. If no resolution, keep contacting institution every 3–6 months. If no response after prolonged period, consider contacting other authorities (eg, ORI in US, GMC in UK) and consider rejecting affected manuscripts and informing authors and institutions. Inform readers and victims of outcome/action where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redundant publication: assess overlap and act accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: When redundancy is reported, check extent and nature of overlap (major overlap vs minor/legitimate overlap) and decide between correction, rejection, or retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use text‑matching software (eg, Crossref similarity Check) to detect redundancy. For major overlap (same data/very similar findings or evidence authors sought to hide redundancy): contact corresponding author with documentary evidence, attempt to contact all authors, consider rejection or retraction and inform author’s institution/superior. For minor/legitimate overlap (eg, methods, translations, re‑analysis): request missing reference to original and/or removal of overlapping material, consider correction that references the original, and inform reviewer/reader of actions. If no response, escalate to authors’ institutions and keep contacting every 3–6 months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of systematic manipulation of the publication process
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic manipulation is where individuals/groups repeatedly use dishonest or fraudulent practices across more than one manuscript (and possibly more than one journal) to influence the publication record and/or achieve financial gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: peer review manipulation (fabricated reviewer identities/emails and submission of favourable reviews), authorship for sale/papermills (inserting accomplished guest authors then replacing or selling authorship), submission/substitution of manuscripts (high‑quality manuscript submitted then substituted for poorer manuscript after acceptance), and publishing fabricated or plagiarised research. Recognise that third‑party editing agencies may be involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognised signs of systematic publication manipulation (red flags)
rubrics_metrics.description: List of features or patterns that may indicate organised manipulation of the publication process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Red flags include: substantial unrequested content changes during revision/after acceptance; article submitted by a third party; same peer reviewers frequently used (fast reviews, brief positive reviews); multiple similar manuscripts in short period (template‑like); numerous manuscripts from same country/institution in short timeframe; suspicious/non‑institutional email addresses; numerous manuscripts with plagiarism/nonsense text; many authorship changes (especially after acceptance); manuscripts on unrelated topics reviewed by same reviewers; shared email addresses or IP patterns. Often a combination of these features indicates concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to investigate suspected publication manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical investigative steps for editors/publishers on discovering suspicious patterns suggesting manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial considerations: determine cause (authors or reviewers) and whether submission system weakness exists. Further investigation might include: searching for IP addresses to check if submissions originate from same location; searching for other submissions/publications by the same authors; cross‑publisher pattern checking via COPE Publishers’ Forum; checking peer reviewers of suspicious manuscripts and published articles; checking reviewer email addresses; checking for requests to change authorship or major revisions after acceptance. Seek advice from COPE. Prevention steps include using technology (flags, searches across journals), training editors to recognise manipulation, and cross‑publisher sharing of patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate actions when suspicion is raised for a submitted manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: If suspicion of systematic manipulation is raised for a submitted manuscript, suspend the peer review process and gather evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suspend peer review if suspicion is raised (eg, suspicious reviewer emails). Get full documentary evidence and try to elucidate whether there is clear evidence of systematic manipulation. Follow existing COPE guidelines and flowcharts. Contact the corresponding author (and co‑authors if possible) with evidence and request an explanation. If no/inconclusive reply, consider contacting authors’ institutions requesting investigation and inform authors. If misconduct is confirmed, consider rejecting manuscripts, and if already published consider retraction; if unclear but unresolved, consider publishing an Expression of Concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer reviewer invitation: criteria for accepting or declining
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist for reviewers when receiving an invitation: legitimacy of journal, understanding review model, conflicts of interest, expertise, time availability, and author identification (for double‑blind).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check if the journal is legitimate (eg, see thinkchecksubmit.org). Read reviewer instructions and confirm you understand and accept the review model and policies. If you cannot or do not accept the model, decline. Check whether author information is provided (and for double‑blind whether you can guess authors). Check for conflicts of interest (professional, personal, financial); if conflicts exist, contact the editor to discuss minimisation or decline. Consider whether you have the necessary expertise to assess the manuscript and whether you can meet the deadline; if not, decline and suggest alternatives. If all checks pass, accept the invitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifying reviewer identity when a legitimate name but suspicious email is provided
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure when a reviewer name appears legitimate but the provided email address is non‑institutional or suspicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify the reviewer at their organisation (check publication record, online search, reviewer databases) to find independent contact details. Contact the named reviewer on an organisational email and ask if they also use the provided address. If reviewer can independently confirm manuscript details and explanation is satisfactory, thank them and continue investigating. If explanation unsatisfactory or no response, contact the individual who suggested the reviewer (eg, handling editor) for explanation. Consider inviting an additional reviewer, contacting the author and institution in neutral terms, or rejecting the manuscript and explaining to author and institution if manipulation is evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognised features/patterns of questionable reviewer activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific behaviours by reviewers that may indicate manipulation or compromised review activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features include: reviewer reports that are very similar to other reports (from purportedly different individuals); third‑party agency involvement; use of non‑institutional emails (gmail/yahoo/hotmail); reviews that are vague in style not matching claimed seniority; overly positive reviews in contrast with others; complimentary reviews that only point out minor technical issues; suspicious email addresses or fictitious names; reviewers working in unrelated subjects; atypical IP address features; extremely quick agreement to review; never recommending rejection; reviews frequently returned well ahead of deadline; agreeing to review many manuscripts and being ‘active’ in a journal database. These features in combination are most suspicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best practices to minimise peer review manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Preventive measures journals should take to reduce peer review manipulation risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require authors to submit manuscripts themselves rather than third parties. Prefer institutional emails or institutionally verified ORCIDs when inviting peer reviewers. Always check that suggested peer reviewers are qualified to review the manuscript and that their email address is accurate. Check for unusual patterns of behaviour across submissions that might indicate manipulation. Provide information and training for editors to raise awareness of manipulation types and what to look out for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal management: editorial office organisation and core principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria for an editorial office to comply with COPE guidelines and best practice in handling ethical issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journal guidelines and processes must be transparent. Systems must be in place to promptly attend to and resolve complaints related to publication ethics. Editorial staff must be committed to correcting the literature when needed and following through on institutional investigation requests. Provide links to COPE guidance and other resources (eg, ICMJE), clearly identify contact information for the person responsible for handling allegations, establish who responds to complaints and within what timeframes, know when/how to liaise with other editors and institutions, and assure access to resources such as retraction guidance, flowcharts, and legal advice if needed. Consider developing training programmes for editors using eLearning or other resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organising editorial office compliance and improvement steps
rubrics_metrics.description: How journals (new or established) should begin auditing and developing processes to meet COPE core practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New journals should begin with COPE Core practices and guidelines from the publisher; established journals should begin with the ‘COPE Journal audit’. Develop guidelines for authors and reviewers based on COPE Core practices (eg, authorship and contributorship, peer review processes). Develop internal processes to support identification of ethical concerns (eg, allegations of misconduct, conflicts of interest, data reproducibility, ethical oversight, intellectual property, journal management, post‑publication corrections). Based on audit results, develop or locate resources to address issues (eg, clarify authorship criteria, update instructions to authors, implement training).
